stem: A 42-year-old woman has right eye pain, blurred vision, and a drooping right eyelid. The right pupil is 6 mm and the left is 3 mm. The right pupil does not constrict to light in either eye, but extraocular movements are normal. CTA shows an aneurysm. Which vessel is most likely involved, and why are the pupillary fibers affected before the eye muscles?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Posterior communicating artery; parasympathetic fibers lie in the center of CN III
Posterior communicating artery; parasympathetic fibers lie on the outer surface of CN III
Anterior communicating artery; sympathetic fibers lie on the outer surface of CN III
Middle cerebral artery; parasympathetic fibers lie in the center of CN III
Superior cerebellar artery; sympathetic fibers lie in the center of CN III

explanation: Painful, pupil-involving CN III palsy (ptosis with a dilated 6 mm nonreactive pupil sparing extraocular motility initially) is classic for compression by a posterior communicating artery (PCom) aneurysm. Parasympathetic fibers controlling pupillary constriction travel along the superficial outer surface of CN III, making them vulnerable to external aneurysmal compression before deeper somatic motor fibers.

stem: A 36-year-old man with AIDS (CD4 count 70/µL) has 3 weeks of progressive right hemiparesis and a visual field defect. MRI shows nonenhancing T2-hyperintense subcortical white matter lesions without mass effect, and CSF JC virus PCR is positive. Which management and associated risk are correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine; response expected within 2 weeks
Methotrexate and radiation; median survival of 3–4 months
Start antiretroviral therapy; risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome
IV acyclovir; hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe
Amphotericin B and flucytosine; elevated intracranial pressure

explanation: In AIDS-associated PML, the only effective therapy is immune restoration with antiretroviral therapy (ART), which stabilizes or improves lesions in roughly half of patients; however, starting ART carries a substantial risk of triggering CNS Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS).

stem: A 55-year-old woman takes a first-line drug for focal seizures that she also uses for trigeminal neuralgia. She develops fatigue and headache. Serum sodium is 124 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is inappropriately high, and she is euvolemic. Which drug and mechanism of hyponatremia are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Phenytoin; adrenal insufficiency
Ethosuximide; renal salt wasting
Carbamazepine; SIADH free-water retention
Lamotrigine; nephrogenic diuresis
Valproic acid; primary polydipsia

explanation: Euvolemic hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine defines SIADH. Carbamazepine (first-line for trigeminal neuralgia and focal seizures) potentiates ADH release and renal water reabsorption, causing hyponatremia.

stem: A 54-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is admitted with confusion and a serum sodium of 106 mEq/L. Sodium is corrected to 128 mEq/L within 24 hours. Four days later he is quadriparetic with dysarthria and dysphagia, and he can communicate only by blinking and moving his eyes vertically. Which is the most likely underlying process?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Thrombotic basilar artery occlusion
Osmotic demyelination of basis pontis
JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes
Acute Wernicke thiamine deficiency
Acute demyelinating pontine MS plaque

explanation: Rapid correction of severe hyponatremia causes osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis) of the basis pontis, producing quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and a locked-in picture. The history of fast correction separates it from basilar thrombosis.

stem: A 61-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden horizontal double vision. His left eye is turned medially and cannot abduct. He has right arm and leg weakness with a Babinski sign, a right lower facial droop with forehead sparing, tongue deviation to the right, loss of light touch on the right body, and loss of pain and temperature on the right face. Which explains the tongue deviation, and which artery is occluded?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Left hypoglossal nucleus; anterior spinal artery
Right hypoglossal nucleus; paramedian basilar artery
Left corticobulbar UMN lesion; paramedian basilar artery
Right corticobulbar tract; posterior cerebral artery
Left nucleus ambiguus lesion; posterior cerebellar artery

explanation: Ipsilateral CN VI palsy (failure to abduct the left eye), contralateral (right) UMN hemiparesis, contralateral lower facial droop, contralateral tongue deviation, contralateral dorsal-column touch loss, and (per course ventral trigeminothalamic tract slides) contralateral facial pain/temperature loss localize to a medial inferior pontine infarct supplied by paramedian branches of the basilar artery. The left-sided corticobulbar lesion removes UMN innervation to the right genioglossus, causing the tongue to deviate contralaterally (to the right).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 16-year-old boy has severe headache, low-grade fever, and diplopia a few days after surgical drainage of a right midface furuncle. He has right periorbital edema, chemosis, ptosis, weakness of the right eye in all directions, and an absent right corneal reflex, with bilateral papilledema. Which diagnosis best explains these findings, and which nerve involvement explains the absent corneal reflex?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis; CN VII palsy
Acute bacterial orbital cellulitis; CN II ischemia
Posterior communicating aneurysm; CN III injury
Cavernous sinus thrombosis; CN V3 nerve division
Cavernous sinus thrombosis; CN V1 nerve division

explanation: Spreading infection from a dangerous-triangle midface furuncle causing periorbital edema, chemosis, ptosis, complete ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI), papilledema, and loss of the right corneal reflex (afferent limb via ophthalmic division V1) is diagnostic of cavernous sinus thrombosis. V1 and V2 traverse the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, whereas V3 exits through the foramen ovale without entering the sinus.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with relapsing neurologic symptoms reports double vision when looking to the right. On rightward gaze her left eye fails to adduct and her right eye shows abducting nystagmus. Convergence is intact. Which structure is demyelinated?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Right abducens nerve nucleus in pons
Right medial longitudinal fasciculus
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Left oculomotor nerve nucleus in midbrain
Right paramedian pontine reticular center

explanation: Failure of one eye to adduct, abducting nystagmus in the other eye, and intact convergence define internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The lesion is in the MLF on the same side as the eye that cannot adduct (left). Intact convergence excludes the oculomotor nucleus or nerve, and an abducens nucleus or PPRF lesion would cause a conjugate gaze palsy.

stem: A 66-year-old man has sudden diplopia and clumsiness. His right eye is down and out with ptosis and a dilated pupil. He has left limb ataxia on finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing and mild slowness and stiffness of the left arm. Strength and sensation are normal, the face is symmetric, and the tongue is midline. Which syndrome, structure, and artery best fit?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Weber syndrome; right cerebral peduncle and basis; PCA
Wallenberg syndrome; left inferior cerebellar peduncle; PICA
Benedikt syndrome; medial lemniscus and VTT tract; PCA
Claude syndrome; right red nucleus and SCP fibers; PCA
Dejerine syndrome; left medullary pyramid; anterior spinal

explanation: Ipsilateral CN III palsy paired with contralateral cerebellar limb ataxia (intention tremor, dysmetria) and mild extrapyramidal slowness/stiffness—while sparing corticospinal strength and medial lemniscus sensation—characterizes Claude syndrome, caused by PCA occlusion affecting the red nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle fibers in the midbrain tegmentum.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 58-year-old man has sudden vertigo, nausea, and nystagmus, and he falls when he tries to sit or stand without support. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin are normal. MRI shows an infarct of the flocculonodular lobe. Which deep nucleus and peduncle carry the principal connection of this part of the cerebellum?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Dentate nucleus; superior cerebellar peduncle
Interposed nuclei; superior cerebellar peduncle
Dentate nucleus; middle cerebellar peduncle
Fastigial nucleus; middle cerebellar peduncle
Fastigial nucleus; inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: The flocculonodular lobe is the vestibulocerebellum. It connects with the vestibular nuclei and the fastigial nucleus through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, and lesions cause vertigo, nystagmus, and truncal instability.

stem: A 40-year-old man has depression, cognitive decline, and involuntary writhing movements. His father died in an institution with a similar illness. MRI shows caudate and putamen atrophy. Which pairing of genetic defect, neurochemical state, and drug for the chorea is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: CAG repeat expansion; dopamine loss; levodopa
CAG repeat expansion; relative DA excess; tetrabenazine
GAA repeat expansion; dopamine excess; tetrabenazine
CAG repeat expansion; ACh excess; donepezil
CGG repeat expansion; dopamine deficiency; levodopa

explanation: Autosomal dominant chorea, psychiatric depression/behavioral decline, cognitive deterioration, and striatal (caudate and putamen) atrophy diagnose Huntington disease. It results from a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT; striatal GABA/enkephalin neuron loss leaves a relative excess of dopamine over acetylcholine, and chorea is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors such as tetrabenazine (or deutetrabenazine).

stem: A 72-year-old woman with 3 years of insidiously progressive loss of recent memory, word-finding difficulty, and getting lost in familiar places has hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI. Her family asks about symptomatic treatment, and a drug is started that modestly improves cognition but causes nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal cramping. Which pairing correctly gives its mechanism and a second drug class that can be added?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Dopamine agonism; add a presynaptic VMAT2 inhibitor
VMAT2 inhibition; add an oral cholinesterase inhibitor
NMDA blockade; add an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition; add NMDA antagonist
Serotonin reuptake blockade; add amyloid antibody

explanation: First-line symptomatic agents in Alzheimer disease (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, boosting cortical ACh but commonly causing peripheral muscarinic GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea, cramping). In moderate-to-severe disease, an NMDA receptor antagonist (memantine) can be added.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has episodes of severe dizziness when she tilts her head to the left and has trouble lying on her left side. Hearing is normal. With her head back and left ear down, she develops nausea and rotatory nystagmus. Which type of ataxia is this, and which pairing of cause and treatment is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Cerebellar ataxia from vermis degeneration; physical therapy
Vestibular ataxia from displaced otoliths; Epley maneuver
Sensory ataxia from dorsal column loss; oral vitamin B12
Vestibular ataxia from endolymphatic hydrops; shunt surgery
Cerebellar ataxia from hemispheric mass; Epley maneuver

explanation: Position-triggered vertigo, normal hearing, and rotatory nystagmus on the Dix-Hallpike maneuver indicate BPPV, a peripheral vestibular ataxia. Displaced otoliths in a semicircular canal are the cause, and the Epley maneuver is the treatment.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped taking warfarin has sudden aphasia and right hemiplegia. He was last seen normal 2 hours ago. Blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg, glucose is normal, and INR is 1.0. Non-contrast head CT shows no hemorrhage. Which is the most appropriate next step?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Oral aspirin daily and home observation
Continuous intravenous heparin infusion
Lower blood pressure below 120/80 mm Hg first
Withhold therapy until follow-up brain MRI
IV alteplase now and CTA for thrombectomy

explanation: This patient meets criteria for IV thrombolysis (ischemic stroke onset 2 hours ago within the 4.5-hour window, non-contrast CT negative for hemorrhage, INR 1.0 <= 1.7, BP < 185/110 mm Hg, normal glucose). Give IV alteplase immediately and obtain CT angiography (CTA) to evaluate for large-vessel occlusion amenable to mechanical thrombectomy.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: Which of the following patients with acute ischemic stroke is NOT a candidate for IV thrombolysis?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: A 72-year-old man last known well 2 hours ago, blood pressure 170/95 mm Hg
A 66-year-old woman last known well 3.5 hours ago, glucose 140 mg/dL
An 80-year-old man last known well 3 hours ago, taking daily aspirin
A 59-year-old woman last known well 2 hours ago, therapeutic on warfarin with INR 2.4
A 71-year-old man last known well 4 hours ago, with no hemorrhage on CT

explanation: Therapeutic anticoagulation on warfarin with an INR > 1.7 (here 2.4) is an absolute contraindication to IV thrombolysis with alteplase due to prohibitive hemorrhage risk. Blood pressure 170/95 (< 185/110), daily aspirin, moderate hyperglycemia (140 mg/dL), and onset 3.5–4 hours after last known well (within 4.5 hours) do not contraindicate IV alteplase.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 72-year-old woman has 3 years of insidiously progressive loss of recent memory, word-finding difficulty, and getting lost in familiar places. MRI shows hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy. Which pairing of histopathology and neurochemical deficit is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: α-Synuclein cortical Lewy bodies; nigral dopamine loss
Tau-positive Pick bodies; dorsal raphe serotonin loss
Amyloid plaques and tau tangles; Meynert ACh deficit
Cortical spongiform vacuolation; widespread GABA loss
Striatal caudate atrophy; excessive nigral dopamine

explanation: Insidious progressive episodic memory loss, anomia, and visuospatial disorientation with hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy describe Alzheimer disease. Classic neuropathology demonstrates extracellular β-amyloid (neuritic) plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles, paired with degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the basal nucleus of Meynert.

stem: A 70-year-old man has sudden loss of sensation over the right upper limb. He speaks fluently but uses made-up words and unrelated phrases, and he cannot follow verbal commands. Which aphasia and vascular supply are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Broca aphasia; superior division of the left MCA
Conduction aphasia; arcuate fasciculus
Anomic aphasia; many cortical areas
Wernicke aphasia; inferior division of the left MCA
Transcortical motor aphasia; ACA–MCA watershed

explanation: Fluent speech filled with paraphasias and neologisms, severely impaired comprehension, and right upper-limb cortical sensory loss localize to the posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area) and adjacent parietal cortex supplied by the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 64-year-old man has weakness of both shoulders and upper arms with relatively preserved distal strength after prolonged hypotension during cardiac surgery. Which territory and mechanism are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: MCA M1 trunk; cardiogenic thromboembolism
ACA–MCA borderzone; systemic hypoperfusion
Basilar trunk; in situ atherosclerotic thrombosis
Bilateral PCA; paradoxical venous thromboemboli
Lenticulostriate vessels; chronic lipohyalinosis

explanation: Bilateral proximal shoulder and upper-arm weakness sparing distal hand and leg strength ('man-in-a-barrel' syndrome) following systemic hypotension during cardiac surgery reflects watershed infarction of the bilateral ACA–MCA borderzone territories, which are the most distal and vulnerable perfusion zones.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 30-year-old man has a generalized convulsion lasting 8 minutes. IV lorazepam is given, but the seizure continues, so IV fosphenytoin (a prodrug of phenytoin) is administered. Which mechanism describes the active drug?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Selective thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channel blockade
Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase
Binding presynaptic vesicle glycoprotein SV2A
Use-dependent voltage-gated Na⁺ channel blockade
Increased GABA-A chloride channel opening rate

explanation: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug converted to phenytoin in vivo for status epilepticus. Phenytoin acts via use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, binding preferentially to and prolonging the inactivated state to limit high-frequency repetitive neuronal firing.

stem: A 74-year-old man has fluctuating confusion, well-formed visual hallucinations of children in his home, mild bradykinesia and rigidity, and acts out his dreams during sleep. After haloperidol is given for the hallucinations, he becomes severely rigid and unresponsive. Which pairing of pathology and explanation is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Hyperphosphorylated tau; central ACh excess
Extracellular amyloid; excess striatal dopamine
Cortical α-synuclein Lewy bodies; D2 sensitivity
Cortical TDP-43 inclusions; serotonin excess
Misfolded prion protein; malignant hyperthermia

explanation: Fluctuating cognition, well-formed recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder, and catastrophic worsening of rigidity after a D2-blocking antipsychotic (haloperidol) are hallmarks of dementia with Lewy bodies. Pathology shows cortical and brainstem α-synuclein Lewy bodies, and patients exhibit severe neuroleptic sensitivity.

stem: A 34-year-old man with AIDS was treated for cryptococcal meningitis. Five weeks after starting antiretroviral therapy, he develops worsening headache, fever, and neurologic decline. His CD4 count has risen, his viral load has fallen, and repeat CSF cultures are sterile. Which explanation and management are most appropriate?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Antifungal failure; hold antiretroviral therapy
HIV neurocognitive decline; add second ART agent
Immune reconstitution syndrome; continue ART and steroids
Toxoplasma reactivation; initiate pyrimethamine
CMV encephalitis; administer systemic methotrexate

explanation: Clinical worsening 2–8 weeks after initiating ART with rising CD4 count, falling HIV viral load, and sterile repeat CSF cultures indicates paradoxical Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) against residual cryptococcal antigen. Management is to continue ART and antifungal therapy and add corticosteroids for severe CNS inflammation.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has headaches, poor growth, and difficulty seeing. Visual fields show a bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a calcified, cystic suprasellar mass, and cyst fluid at surgery resembles motor oil. Which pairing identifies the tissue of origin and the mechanism of visual loss?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Rathke pouch remnants; optic chiasm crossing fiber compression
Arachnoid cap cells; unilateral optic tract nerve compression
Pituitary corticotrophs; posterior optic radiation compression
Rathke pouch remnants; temporal optic radiation compression
Orbital Schwann cells; anterior intraorbital nerve compression

explanation: A calcified, cystic suprasellar mass with motor-oil fluid in a child is craniopharyngioma, derived from Rathke pouch remnants. It compresses the optic chiasm, damaging crossing nasal retinal fibers and causing bitemporal hemianopia.

stem: An 8-year-old girl has 2 months of unsteady gait and headaches. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar hemispheric mass with an enhancing mural nodule. The tumor is GFAP-positive with a biphasic pattern. Which histologic finding and WHO grade are expected?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Rosenthal fibers with necrosis; WHO grade IV
Rosenthal fibers and granular bodies; WHO grade I
Pseudopalisading tissue necrosis; WHO grade IV
Homer Wright neuroblastic rosettes; WHO grade IV
Perivascular ependymal pseudorosettes; WHO grade I

explanation: A cystic cerebellar mass with a mural nodule in a child is pilocytic astrocytoma: biphasic, GFAP-positive, with Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies. It is WHO grade I with an excellent prognosis.

stem: A 41-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 45/µL) has 2 weeks of headache, fever, and confusion. CSF opening pressure is elevated, and there is a mild mononuclear pleocytosis. Which pairing gives the diagnostic finding and the induction treatment?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Cowdry type A nuclear inclusions; IV acyclovir
Multiple ring-enhancing nodules; pyrimethamine
Encapsulated yeast on India ink; amphotericin B
JC viral DNA in the CSF; antiretroviral regimen
EBV DNA amplified in CSF; high-dose methotrexate

explanation: Subacute fever, headache, confusion, markedly elevated CSF opening pressure, and mild mononuclear pleocytosis in an HIV patient with CD4 < 100/µL are classic for cryptococcal meningoencephalitis (Cryptococcus neoformans). Encapsulated budding yeast is seen on India ink stain (or cryptococcal antigen is positive), and induction therapy is IV amphotericin B plus flucytosine followed by fluconazole. Toxoplasmosis produces ring-enhancing lesions; PML produces nonenhancing white matter lesions with JC virus DNA; PCNSL is EBV-driven.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with generalized tonic-clonic seizures plans pregnancy and is switched from valproic acid to a lower-risk drug that is effective for both focal and generalized seizures. Which mechanism describes the new drug?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channel blockade
Irreversible GABA transaminase block
Presynaptic GABA GAT-1 reuptake block
Allosteric GABA-A receptor potentiation
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channel inactivation

explanation: Lamotrigine is a broad-spectrum antiseizure agent effective for both focal and generalized seizures with a substantially lower teratogenic risk than valproic acid, making it preferred in women planning pregnancy. Its primary mechanism is blockade of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (prolonging inactivation and reducing glutamate release). Ethosuximide (T-type Ca²⁺), vigabatrin (GABA transaminase), tiagabine (GAT-1 reuptake, focal-only and risky in pregnancy), and benzodiazepines/barbiturates (GABA-A potentiation) do not match this profile.

stem: A 74-year-old man has 6 months of gait difficulty with feet that seem stuck to the floor, followed by memory problems and urinary urgency. MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy. Which mechanism and next step are correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Choroid plexus CSF overproduction; acetazolamide
Aqueductal stenosis; third ventriculostomy alone
Impaired arachnoid CSF resorption; tap test then shunt
Tertiary parenchymal neurosyphilis; IV penicillin
Nigrostriatal dopamine loss; oral carbidopa-levodopa

explanation: The triad of magnetic apraxic gait ('feet stuck to the floor'), urinary incontinence/urgency, and cognitive slowing with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy indicates normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), caused by impaired CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations. Diagnosis and candidacy for VP shunting are assessed with a high-volume lumbar puncture tap test (Miller Fisher test) looking for transient gait improvement.

stem: A 25-year-old woman, 4 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, has 3 days of global headache and vomiting, followed by a seizure. She has bilateral papilledema and no focal deficits. Non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense superior sagittal sinus with an adjacent hemorrhage. Which explains the hemorrhage and the papilledema?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Arterial thromboembolism causing reperfusion hemorrhage
Saccular berry aneurysm rupture at arterial branch
Deep hypertensive Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm
Venous sinus congestion and impaired CSF resorption
Traumatic shearing of cortical bridging veins

explanation: A postpartum hypercoagulable woman presenting with severe global headache, vomiting, seizures, bilateral papilledema, and a hyperdense superior sagittal sinus with venous infarction/hemorrhage has cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Elevated venous back-pressure causes venous hemorrhage, while impaired CSF resorption at arachnoid granulations elevates intracranial pressure and produces papilledema.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 7-year-old boy with absence seizures starts a first-line drug. Two weeks later his parents report nausea and abdominal pain, and he is otherwise well. Which pairing of drug and adverse effect is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Valproic acid; painful gingival hyperplasia
Carbamazepine; fetal neural tube anomalies
Phenytoin; acute fulminant hepatotoxicity
Lamotrigine; syndrome of inappropriate ADH
Ethosuximide; GI upset and Stevens-Johnson rash

explanation: Nausea, dyspepsia, and abdominal discomfort are the most common adverse effects of ethosuximide (first-line for isolated absence seizures), along with rare idiosyncratic Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Gingival hyperplasia is classic for phenytoin; neural tube defects for valproate.

stem: A 9-year-old girl has painless loss of vision in the left eye. The left pupil is 6 mm in the dark and 3 mm in the light, with no direct or consensual response when light is shone in the left eye; the right eye responds normally to light in either eye. She has multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and iris hamartomas on slit-lamp exam. MRI shows a left optic nerve mass. Which pairing correctly gives the pupillary finding and the genetic defect?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Left afferent pupillary defect; NF2, chromosome 22, merlin
Left efferent pupillary defect; NF1, chromosome 17, neurofibromin
Left afferent pupillary defect; NF1, chromosome 17, neurofibromin
Right afferent pupillary defect; NF1, chromosome 17, neurofibromin
Left afferent pupillary defect; TSC2, chromosome 16, tuberin

explanation: Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, and an optic nerve glioma indicate NF1 (chromosome 17, neurofibromin). A left optic nerve lesion causes a left afferent pupillary defect: no direct response in the left eye and no consensual response to the right when light is in the left eye, with normal responses when light is in the right.

stem: A 5-year-old child with generalized tonic-clonic and myoclonic seizures has been on a first-line broad-spectrum antiseizure drug for 2 months. He now has lethargy, vomiting, and jaundice, with markedly elevated AST, ALT, and ammonia. Which drug and adverse effect are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Carbamazepine; agranulocytosis
Phenytoin; gingival hyperplasia
Valproic acid; hepatotoxicity
Ethosuximide; abdominal pain
Lamotrigine; Stevens-Johnson syndrome

explanation: Lethargy, vomiting, jaundice, markedly elevated transaminases, and hyperammonemia shortly after starting a broad-spectrum antiseizure drug in a young child point to valproic acid-induced hepatotoxicity (fatal liver failure risk is highest in children under 2 years or on polytherapy).

stem: A 36-year-old man who runs a cat boarding facility has HIV with a CD4 count of 60/µL. He has 1 week of headache and fever, left hemiparesis, and a seizure. MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia. Which diagnosis and treatment are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Primary CNS lymphoma; methotrexate therapy
Cryptococcal meningitis; amphotericin B therapy
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy; ART
Toxoplasma reactivation; pyrimethamine plus sulfa
Cytomegalovirus encephalitis; IV ganciclovir

explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia or corticomedullary junction in an HIV patient with CD4 < 100/µL and cat exposure indicate Toxoplasma gondii reactivation. First-line treatment is pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine (with leucovorin). Primary CNS lymphoma classically presents as a solitary or periventricular homogeneously enhancing lesion crossing the corpus callosum; PML is nonenhancing without mass effect.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with MS reports an electric-shock sensation down her spine when she flexes her neck, and her vision blurs after a hot shower. Which pairing correctly explains these two phenomena?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Lhermitte sign: lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus; Uhthoff phenomenon: increased myelin synthesis with heat
Lhermitte sign: demyelination of the cervical dorsal columns; Uhthoff phenomenon: heat-induced conduction block in demyelinated axons
Lhermitte sign: demyelination of the spinothalamic tract; Uhthoff phenomenon: heat-induced axonal regeneration
Lhermitte sign: peripheral nerve root inflammation; Uhthoff phenomenon: heat-induced antibody release
Lhermitte sign: cerebellar peduncle lesion; Uhthoff phenomenon: heat-induced Schwann cell injury

explanation: Lhermitte sign reflects demyelination of the cervical dorsal columns, producing shocks on neck flexion. Uhthoff phenomenon is worsening of symptoms with heat due to conduction block in demyelinated axons.

stem: A 55-year-old woman repeatedly bumps into cabinet doors on her left and has a left homonymous hemianopia with sparing of central vision. Which artery is occluded, and what explains the macular sparing?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Right MCA; macula localizes to parietal cortex
Left PCA; collateral perfusion from the ACA
Right PCA; collateral MCA supply at occipital pole
Right PCA; macula localizes to temporal cortex
Right choroidal; collateral basilar perfusion

explanation: Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing results from occlusion of the right posterior cerebral artery (PCA) supplying the primary visual cortex. Central/macular vision is spared because the occipital pole receives dual collateral blood supply from the middle cerebral artery (MCA).

stem: A 22-year-old man is struck on the temple by a baseball and briefly loses consciousness. He wakes up and feels well, but 2 hours later he becomes drowsy and develops a dilated pupil. CT shows a biconvex hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines. Which vessel is injured, and at which skull site?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Bridging veins; parietal bone
Superior sagittal sinus; vertex

stem: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her warfarin a month ago. She has diplopia and shaking when reaching. Her right eye is deviated down and out, and the right pupil is 8 mm and unreactive. She has loss of light touch on the left body, loss of touch and pinprick on the left face, and normal strength. There is intention tremor with overshoot in the left arm and leg. Which structure best explains the left limb ataxia, and which artery is involved?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

Left inferior cerebellar peduncle; PICA trunk
Right middle cerebellar peduncle; basilar trunk
Left crus cerebri corticospinal tract; PCA branches
Right superior cerebellar peduncle fibers; PCA branches

explanation: Ipsilateral CN III palsy (right eye down and out, dilated pupil) combined with contralateral (left) cerebellar limb ataxia/intention tremor and contralateral loss of discriminative touch on body/face indicates a midbrain tegmental stroke (Benedikt/Claude spectrum) supplied by PCA branches. Involvement of the right red nucleus and adjacent superior cerebellar peduncle fibers (which already decussated below and project to the right motor cortex) produces contralateral left-sided limb ataxia.

stem: A 44-year-old man with Down syndrome develops progressive memory decline. Which gene on chromosome 21 explains his early-onset Alzheimer disease, and what is its pathogenic consequence?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

PSEN1; decreased γ-secretase enzyme activity
MAPT; hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrils
SNCA; abnormal α-synuclein oligomerization
APP; excess amyloid-β from extra gene dosage

explanation: Individuals with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) carry three copies of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene on chromosome 21, leading to lifelong overproduction and accumulation of amyloid-β and early-onset Alzheimer disease.

stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden right arm and lower face weakness with effortful, telegraphic speech. He understands commands and appears frustrated, but repetition is impaired. Which aphasia and lesion location are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

Conduction aphasia; subcortical arcuate fasciculus
Transcortical sensory aphasia; posterior watershed
Global aphasia; entire dominant perisylvian zone
Broca aphasia; posterior inferior frontal gyrus

explanation: Nonfluent, effortful, telegraphic speech with intact comprehension and impaired repetition, accompanied by right arm and lower facial weakness, localizes to the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area) and adjacent motor strip in the left hemisphere, supplied by the superior division of the left MCA.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is starting lamotrigine for focal seizures. Which counseling about its most serious adverse effect is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Monthly blood counts for marrow agranulocytosis
High-dose folate to block neural tube defects
Titrate slowly and stop immediately if rash appears
Frequent serum sodium checks for drug SIADH
Regular dental cleanings for gingival overgrowth

explanation: Patients starting lamotrigine must be counseled to follow a slow upward titration schedule (especially with concurrent valproate) and to stop the medication immediately and seek urgent medical evaluation at the first sign of rash, fever, or mucosal lesions to prevent progression to Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has right hemiparesis and aphasia from a left MCA occlusion. Within minutes, neurons in the ischemic core fail to generate enough ATP. Which sequence best describes the excitotoxic cascade that follows?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase overdrive, neuronal hyperpolarization, excess GABA release
Enhanced glutamate reuptake, NMDA blockade, cellular ATP preservation
Na⁺/K⁺ pump failure, glutamate release, Ca²⁺ influx, free radicals
Potassium channel opening, cell shrinkage, calcium-free apoptosis
Mitochondrial uncoupling, ATP surge, compensatory NMDA inhibition

explanation: During acute focal ischemia, ATP depletion impairs Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, causing neuronal depolarization and massive presynaptic glutamate release. Glutamate activates AMPA and NMDA receptors, driving excessive intracellular Ca²⁺ influx that activates proteases, lipases, endonucleases, and free radical formation, culminating in cell death.

stem: A 16-year-old has myoclonic jerks on awakening and one generalized tonic-clonic seizure. EEG shows generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges. A broad-spectrum first-line drug is chosen. Which mechanism describes this drug?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Binds presynaptic synaptic vesicle protein SV2A
Selectively inhibits thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channels
Selectively blocks inactivated voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Blocks Na⁺ and T-type Ca²⁺ channels and elevates GABA
Prolongs opening duration of GABA-A chloride channels

explanation: Morning myoclonic jerks and generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a teenager with generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges represent juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME). Valproic acid is the classic broad-spectrum first-line agent, acting via blockade of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and T-type Ca²⁺ channels plus inhibition of GABA transaminase/SSADH to raise brain GABA.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a 15-year history of alcohol use disorder has a 5-month history of gait disturbance. She walks with a wide-based gait and sways from side to side when sitting unsupported. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin are normal, vibration and proprioception are intact, and nystagmus and vertigo are absent. Which structure is most likely affected?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Flocculonodular cerebellar lobe
Left lateral cerebellar hemisphere
Anterior cerebellar vermis
Deep cerebellar dentate nucleus
Spinal dorsal column tracts

explanation: Truncal ataxia with normal limb testing localizes to the vermis (spinocerebellum), which atrophies with chronic alcohol use. Flocculonodular lesions cause vertigo and nystagmus, and hemispheric lesions cause limb ataxia.

stem: A 39-year-old man with AIDS (CD4 count 25/µL) has 1 week of severe low back pain radiating to the legs, saddle numbness, urinary retention, and flaccid paraparesis. CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose. Which diagnosis is most likely, and which additional manifestation is typical of this pathogen?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Guillain-Barré syndrome; albuminocytologic CSF
HIV vacuolar myelopathy; dorsal cord vacuolation
Cytomegalovirus polyradiculitis; CMV retinitis
CNS toxoplasmosis; basal ganglia ring lesions
JC virus leukoencephalopathy; white matter change

explanation: Subacute lumbosacral polyradiculopathy (severe radicular low back pain, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and flaccid paraparesis) with polymorphonuclear/neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose in late-stage AIDS (CD4 < 50/µL) is classic for CMV polyradiculitis (treat with IV ganciclovir). Another classic CMV manifestation in AIDS is hemorrhagic retinitis.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has morning headaches, vomiting, and diplopia. MRI shows a mass arising from the floor of the fourth ventricle with obstructive hydrocephalus. Which histologic structure is characteristic of this tumor?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Perivascular pseudorosettes
Homer Wright tumor rosettes
Whorls with psammoma bodies
Palisading Verocay bodies
Thickened Rosenthal fibers

explanation: A fourth-ventricle floor tumor in a child with hydrocephalus is ependymoma, showing perivascular pseudorosettes. Homer Wright rosettes are medulloblastoma, whorls with psammoma bodies are meningioma, Verocay bodies are schwannoma, and Rosenthal fibers are pilocytic astrocytoma.

stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV has 1 year of poor concentration, slowed thinking, mild short-term memory lapses, and clumsiness with fine hand movements and gait. MRI shows nonspecific subcortical white matter changes, and CSF has no organism. Which statement is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: It presents as cortical dementia with severe aphasia
It is subcortical HIV dementia diagnosed by exclusion
Multiple ring-enhancing basal lesions are expected
Immediate empiric IV acyclovir therapy is required
It results from JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes

explanation: Slowed information processing, poor concentration, apathy, mild memory retrieval deficits, clumsiness/gait slowing, nonspecific subcortical white matter changes, and sterile CSF represent HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND). Unlike Alzheimer disease, HAND has a subcortical dementia pattern without prominent cortical aphasia/apraxia and remains a diagnosis of exclusion.

stem: A 47-year-old man with HIV has painful burning paresthesias in a stocking distribution. He has been taking stavudine and didanosine for 2 years. Exam shows reduced pinprick sensation and absent ankle reflexes bilaterally with normal strength; CSF is normal. Which diagnosis and management are most appropriate?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: CMV polyradiculitis; initiate IV ganciclovir
Guillain-Barré syndrome; start plasma exchange
HIV vacuolar myelopathy; high-dose steroids
NRTI distal neuropathy; supportive drug review
Cerebral toxoplasmosis; start pyrimethamine

explanation: Symmetric painful burning paresthesias in a stocking distribution with reduced pinprick and absent ankle jerks in an HIV patient taking stavudine (d4T) or didanosine (ddI) are classic for NRTI-induced mitochondrial toxic distal symmetric polyneuropathy. Management consists of supportive neuropathic pain care and reviewing/switching the offending nucleoside analogue.

stem: A 53-year-old man has a new generalized seizure. After recovery he is oriented with no neurologic deficits. MRI shows a large ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and surrounding edema that crosses the corpus callosum. Which histologic finding is expected on biopsy?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Pseudopalisading necrosis with microvascular proliferation
Whorled spindle cells with psammoma bodies
Perinuclear halos with a chicken-wire capillary network
Small round blue cells forming Homer Wright rosettes
Rosenthal fibers with eosinophilic granular bodies

explanation: A ring-enhancing necrotic mass crossing the corpus callosum is glioblastoma, which shows pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation (GFAP-positive, often EGFR amplified). B is meningioma, C is oligodendroglioma, D is medulloblastoma, and E is pilocytic astrocytoma.

stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation suddenly develops vertigo and nausea. The entire left face is drooped, including the forehead, and he cannot close his left eye. He has loss of pain and temperature on the left face and the right body, a small left pupil with ptosis, and left limb ataxia. Strength is normal and the tongue is midline. Which artery is occluded, and which finding best distinguishes this from lateral medullary syndrome?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: PICA trunk; ipsilateral Horner syndrome findings
PCA branches; contralateral hemiparesis weakness
Anterior spinal; ipsilateral tongue deviation
AICA trunk; complete ipsilateral facial paralysis
Vertebral artery; contralateral limb ataxia

explanation: Vertigo, nausea, ipsilateral pain/temperature loss on the face, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and ipsilateral ataxia overlap with Wallenberg syndrome, but complete ipsilateral facial paralysis (including the forehead, LMN CN VII) pinpoints lateral inferior pontine infarction from occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA).

stem: A 66-year-old smoker has 5 minutes of painless vision loss in the right eye, like a curtain falling, which then resolves completely. Carotid duplex shows 80% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery. Which cause and management are most appropriate?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Inflammatory optic neuritis; IV methylprednisolone
Acute retinal detachment; emergent laser photocoagulation
ICA atheroembolism TIA; endarterectomy, aspirin, statin
Giant cell arteritis; outpatient observation alone
Atrial fibrillation embolism; warfarin monotherapy

explanation: Painless transient monocular vision loss ('curtain falling', amaurosis fugax) lasting minutes in a patient with 80% ipsilateral ICA stenosis is a retinal TIA caused by atheroembolism from the carotid plaque to the ophthalmic and central retinal arteries. Because ipsilateral stenosis is >= 70% (symptomatic), carotid endarterectomy plus antiplatelet therapy and a high-intensity statin are indicated.

stem: A 78-year-old man with chronic alcohol use fell 3 weeks ago and now has headache and progressive confusion. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines. Which vessel was torn, and what is the expected CT shape?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

Bridging veins; crescent-shaped, crossing sutures
Lenticulostriate artery; round and intraparenchymal
Berry aneurysm; star-shaped within the cisterns
Superior sagittal sinus; biconvex

explanation: Subacute headache and cognitive decline weeks after a minor fall in an older patient with chronic alcohol use (cerebral atrophy stretching bridging veins) with a crescent-shaped hematoma crossing suture lines describes a chronic subdural hematoma from torn bridging cortical veins.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 38-year-old woman was diagnosed with MS at age 25 after episodes of optic neuritis and leg weakness that each resolved. Over the past 3 years she has had steady worsening of gait with no clear relapses or recovery. Which MS course does she now have?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Clinically isolated syndrome
Relapsing-remitting MS course
Primary progressive MS course
Secondary progressive MS
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum

explanation: MS usually begins as relapsing-remitting and later converts to secondary progressive (often more than 10 years after diagnosis), with steady worsening without clear relapses. Primary progressive MS is progressive from onset.

stem: A 45-year-old man with AIDS (CD4 count 30/µL) has insidious confusion and personality change. MRI shows a single homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum. Toxoplasma IgG is negative. CSF shows elevated protein, LDH, and β2-microglobulin. Which virus is associated with this tumor, and which test supports the diagnosis?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: HHV-8; HHV-8 serology
JC virus; JC virus PCR in CSF
EBV; EBV PCR in CSF
CMV; CMV PCR in CSF
HSV-1; HSV PCR in CSF

explanation: An AIDS patient with CD4 < 50/µL, a single homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum, negative Toxoplasma IgG, and elevated CSF LDH and β2-microglobulin has AIDS-related primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL). PCNSL in HIV is almost universally associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and CSF EBV PCR supports the diagnosis.

stem: A 12-year-old develops fever, mucosal erosions, and widespread skin sloughing 3 weeks after starting an antiseizure drug. Which adverse effect is shared by carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and ethosuximide?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Fulminant hepatotoxicity
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Hemorrhagic pancreatitis
Drug-induced gum hypertrophy
Fetal neural tube defects

explanation: Fever, mucosal erosions, and widespread epidermal sloughing indicate Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS/TEN), a severe mucocutaneous hypersensitivity reaction that is a shared idiosyncratic risk across carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and ethosuximide (as well as phenytoin).

stem: A 58-year-old woman after a left parietal infarct speaks fluently and understands commands, but she cannot repeat “no ifs, ands, or buts.” She makes paraphasic errors and has trouble naming. Which structure is most likely damaged?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Arcuate fasciculus tract
Inferior frontal Broca area
Posterior superior temporal gyrus
Medial supplementary motor cortex
Posterior limb of internal capsule

explanation: Conduction aphasia—characterized by fluent speech, intact auditory comprehension, paraphasic/naming errors, and markedly impaired repetition—is classically caused by a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus (part of the superior longitudinal fasciculus) connecting Wernicke and Broca areas.

stem: A 33-year-old man has 4 days of progressive leg weakness and tingling. Four weeks ago he had diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken. Strength is 4/5 at the knees and 3/5 at the ankles bilaterally, and patellar and ankle reflexes are absent. Which pairing of pathogenesis and expected CSF findings is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Molecular mimicry to peripheral myelin; neutrophilic CSF and low glucose
Antibodies to postsynaptic ACh receptors; normal CSF protein and cells
Antibodies to astrocytic aquaporin-4; intrathecal oligoclonal IgG bands
Molecular mimicry to peripheral myelin; high protein with normal WBCs
JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes; viral DNA detected in the CSF

explanation: Ascending areflexic weakness 1–3 weeks after Campylobacter jejuni enteritis is Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP). Antibodies and T cells cross-react with Schwann cell and myelin antigens (molecular mimicry), and CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cells).

stem: An 80-year-old woman suddenly ignores her left side. She puts only her right arm in her sleeve, eats only food on the right side of her plate, and draws a clock with all the numbers on the right. She is unaware of any problem. Which lesion and additional visual deficit are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Left parietal lobe via MCA; right hemianopia
Right parietal lobe via MCA; left hemianopia
Right occipital pole via PCA; macular sparing
Left frontal cortex via ACA; intact visual fields
Right thalamus via PCA; bitemporal hemianopia

explanation: Acute left hemispatial neglect (dressing only the right arm, eating only from the right half of the plate, drawing all clock numbers on the right) and anosognosia localize to the nondominant (right) posterior parietal lobe supplied by the MCA. Damage to the adjacent superior optic radiations produces a left inferior quadrantanopia or left homonymous hemianopia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 60-year-old man has sudden weakness of the entire right side of his body with hyperreflexia, increased tone, a right lower facial droop, and tongue protrusion to the right. He also has right-sided dysmetria and intention tremor. MRI shows an infarct of the middle and medial parts of the left crus cerebri. Which additional finding is expected, and what explains the right-sided ataxia?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Right oculomotor palsy; lesion of the right cerebellar hemisphere cortex
Left abducens palsy; interruption of crossed left dentatorubral fibers
Left oculomotor palsy; interruption of left frontopontine tract fibers
Right complete facial palsy; damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle
Left hypoglossal palsy; interruption of ascending spinocerebellar tracts

explanation: The crus cerebri carries corticospinal, corticobulbar, and frontopontine fibers, and CN III fibers pass nearby, so a left lesion gives a left oculomotor palsy. Right-sided ataxia arises from interruption of the left frontopontine fibers of the cerebrocerebellar circuit (cortex to pons to the right cerebellum).

stem: A 44-year-old man with untreated AIDS has 6 months of slowly progressive, painless gait disturbance, neurogenic bladder, spastic paraparesis, and loss of vibration and proprioception in the legs. Vitamin B12 level, syphilis serologies, and HTLV-1 testing are negative. Which spinal region and process are most likely involved?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Thoracic spinal cord; vacuolar myelopathy
Cervical spinal cord; central syringomyelia
Lumbosacral roots; CMV polyradiculitis
Conus medullaris; CNS toxoplasma abscess
Distal nerves; symmetric sensory neuropathy

explanation: Slowly progressive, painless spastic paraparesis, neurogenic bladder, and loss of dorsal column modalities (vibration and proprioception) over months in untreated advanced AIDS—after excluding B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HTLV-1—is characteristic of HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy, which primarily involves the dorsal and lateral columns of the thoracic spinal cord.

stem: A 66-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has sudden right hemiparesis, headache, and vomiting. CT shows a hyperdense hemorrhage in the left putamen. Which vascular pathology is responsible?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Saccular aneurysm rupture on communicating artery
Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm rupture in basal ganglia
Cortical bridging vein rupture in subdural space
Middle meningeal artery laceration at pterion
Deep cerebral venous sinus septic thrombosis

explanation: Spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the putamen of a patient with chronic poorly controlled hypertension is caused by rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms arising along small penetrating lenticulostriate arteries.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 63-year-old woman has sudden left-sided tongue weakness and right-sided weakness. Her tongue deviates to the left with lower motor neuron signs. She has right arm and leg weakness with a Babinski sign, loss of light touch, vibration, and proprioception on the right body, and loss of pain sensation on the right face. There is no facial droop, vertigo, or Horner syndrome. Which artery is occluded, and which structure explains the tongue findings?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: PICA occlusion; left nucleus ambiguus
AICA occlusion; left facial motor nucleus
PCA occlusion; right corticobulbar fibers
Basilar occlusion; left abducens nerve nucleus
Anterior spinal occlusion; left hypoglossal fibers

explanation: Ipsilateral LMN tongue weakness (deviating to the left), contralateral (right) UMN hemiparesis, contralateral dorsal-column vibration/proprioception loss, and contralateral facial pain loss (attributed in course slides to the ventral trigeminothalamic tract) without vertigo, facial paralysis, or Horner syndrome define medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome caused by anterior spinal artery occlusion injuring the left hypoglossal nucleus/rootlets, pyramid, and medial lemniscus.

stem: A 29-year-old man collapses with a generalized seizure after 2 months of headaches and personality change. MRI shows a calcified frontal lobe mass. Biopsy shows round cells with perinuclear halos and a delicate branching capillary network. Which molecular alteration is characteristic of this tumor?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: EGFR gene amplification
NF2 loss of function
MYC oncogene amplification
1p/19q chromosomal codeletion
VHL tumor suppressor loss

explanation: Fried-egg cells, a chicken-wire capillary network, and calcification in the frontal lobe indicate oligodendroglioma, characterized by 1p/19q codeletion. EGFR amplification is typical of glioblastoma, and NF2 loss is seen in schwannoma and meningioma.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes wakes with double vision. Her right eye is deviated down and out with ptosis and a dilated pupil. She has left arm and leg weakness with increased tone and a Babinski sign, a left lower facial droop with forehead sparing, and tongue deviation to the left. Which artery supplies the infarcted region, and what explains the tongue deviation?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Anterior spinal artery; right hypoglossal nucleus
Posterior inferior cerebellar; left nucleus ambiguus
Posterior cerebral artery; right hypoglossal nerve root
Posterior cerebral branches; right crus corticobulbar
Paramedian basilar; left pontine corticobulbar tract

explanation: Ipsilateral CN III palsy (right eye down and out, ptosis, mydriasis) combined with contralateral (left) UMN hemiparesis, contralateral lower facial droop, and contralateral tongue deviation constitutes Weber syndrome (medial midbrain crus cerebri infarct supplied by penetrating PCA branches). Involvement of corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers in the right crus cerebri disrupts UMN input to contralateral CN VII and XII (causing tongue deviation toward the weak/contralateral left side).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 38-year-old woman has 1 year of progressive right hearing loss and tinnitus, with recent vertigo and right facial numbness. MRI shows an enhancing right cerebellopontine angle mass. Which pairing of cell of origin and histologic hallmark is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Arachnoid cap cells; laminated psammoma bodies
Fibrillary astrocytes; bright Rosenthal fibers
Schwann cells; Antoni A/B areas and Verocay bodies
Ependymal lining cells; perivascular pseudorosettes
Granule cell precursors; Homer Wright rosettes

explanation: A cerebellopontine angle mass with hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, and facial numbness is a vestibular schwannoma. It arises from Schwann cells, is S100-positive, and shows dense Antoni A areas (with Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has 5 days of bilateral visual loss and progressive leg weakness with a T6 sensory level. Spinal MRI shows a T2-hyperintense lesion spanning five vertebral segments; brain MRI is normal. Which is the most likely target of the pathogenic autoantibody?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Gangliosides on peripheral axons
Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel
Peripheral myelin protein 22
Aquaporin-4 on astrocyte end-feet

explanation: Optic neuritis plus a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (three or more segments) with a normal brain MRI is neuromyelitis optica, caused by antibodies to aquaporin-4 on astrocyte end-feet. MS lesions are typically short. Treat attacks with steroids or plasma exchange, and use azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab, or eculizumab long term.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting MS has 3 days of new right arm weakness and spasticity, and MRI shows a new enhancing lesion. Which pairing correctly gives treatment for this acute relapse and an appropriate long-term disease-modifying agent?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: IV methylprednisolone; interferon-β
IV acyclovir therapy; oral fingolimod
Intravenous immune globulin; riluzole
IV methylprednisolone; oral riluzole
Oral baclofen therapy; glatiramer

explanation: Acute MS relapses are treated with IV methylprednisolone, and long-term disease-modifying options include interferon-β and glatiramer acetate (also fingolimod, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and others). Riluzole is for ALS, acyclovir is for HSV, and IVIG and baclofen are not standard relapse therapy.

stem: A 57-year-old hypertensive man has sudden vertigo, vomiting, and hoarseness while mowing the lawn. He has nystagmus, falls toward the left, and has truncal and left limb ataxia. His voice is hoarse, he has dysphagia, and the uvula deviates to the right. He has loss of pain and temperature on the right body and left face, and left ptosis with miosis. Strength is normal. Which artery is occluded, and which structure explains the hoarseness and dysphagia?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Anterior spinal artery; left hypoglossal nucleus
PICA branch occlusion; left nucleus ambiguus
PICA branch occlusion; right nucleus ambiguus
AICA branch occlusion; left facial motor nucleus
Basilar trunk occlusion; bilateral corticobulbar

explanation: Sudden vertigo, falling to the left, left limb ataxia, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and bulbar signs (hoarseness, dysphagia, uvula deviating to the right) define lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome caused by PICA occlusion; damage to the left nucleus ambiguus explains the dysphagia, hoarseness, and palatal weakness.
