stem: An 8-year-old girl has dozens of 10-second staring spells each day with no postictal confusion, reproduced by hyperventilation. EEG shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Which mechanism describes the first-line drug for this seizure type?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Prolongs inactivated state of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Inhibits GABA transaminase to reduce GABA breakdown
Blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels in thalamic neurons
Blocks Na⁺ and T-type Ca²⁺ channels and raises GABA
Directly blocks postsynaptic glutamate NMDA channels

explanation: Brief 10-second staring spells in a child without postictal confusion, provoked by hyperventilation, with 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges on EEG define childhood absence epilepsy. The first-line agent is ethosuximide, which acts by selectively blocking thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channels.

stem: A 2-year-old boy has 3 weeks of daily vomiting, frequent head-holding, and unsteady gait. He is afebrile. Exam shows bilateral papilledema and a wide-based gait, with normal finger-to-nose testing. MRI shows a midline cerebellar mass compressing the fourth ventricle. Which pairing of histology and pattern of spread is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Perivascular pseudorosettes; hematogenous lung dissemination
Eosinophilic Rosenthal fibers; transcallosal brain spread
Homer Wright pseudorosettes; CSF drop spinal metastases
Antoni A and B palisading zones; cranial nerve extension
Meningothelial whorls and psammoma bodies; local dural spread

explanation: A midline cerebellar mass compressing the fourth ventricle in a young child, with papilledema and vomiting from obstructive hydrocephalus, is medulloblastoma. Histology shows small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes, and it spreads through CSF as drop metastases. Normal finger-to-nose fits a midline vermian lesion.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has 4 months of rapidly progressive dementia, startle myoclonus, and ataxia. EEG shows periodic sharp-wave complexes, and CSF is positive for 14-3-3 protein. Which pairing of pathogenic mechanism and histology is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Hyperphosphorylated tau; neurofibrillary tangles
Misfolded α-synuclein; cortical Lewy bodies
Extracellular β-amyloid; neuritic plaques
Polyglutamine huntingtin; caudate striatal loss
PrPc to PrPsc beta conversion; spongiform change

explanation: Rapidly progressive dementia over months with startle myoclonus, ataxia, periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, and positive CSF 14-3-3 protein is classic for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Prion disease involves conformational conversion of normal α-helical cellular prion protein (PrPc) into protease-resistant β-sheet scrapie prion (PrPsc), causing neuronal loss, gliosis, and cortical spongiform vacuolation without an inflammatory infiltrate.

stem: A 64-year-old man has sudden weakness of the left leg with hyperreflexia and increased tone, decreased touch and pinprick sensation in the left leg, and new urinary incontinence. The arm and face are spared. Which artery is occluded, and which cortical region is involved?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Left ACA; medial frontal motor cortex
Right MCA; lateral frontal convexity
Right ACA; medial frontal paracentral lobule
Right PCA; medial occipital visual cortex
Right choroidal; posterior internal capsule

explanation: Contralateral (left) leg weakness with UMN signs, contralateral leg sensory loss, and urinary incontinence sparing the face and arm localize to the right paracentral lobule and medial frontal lobe supplied by the right anterior cerebral artery (ACA).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 40-year-old man with episodes of a rising epigastric sensation followed by lip-smacking and unresponsiveness starts a Na⁺ channel–blocking first-line drug. Three weeks later he has fever and sore throat, and his absolute neutrophil count is 200/µL. Which drug and adverse effect are most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Valproic acid; acute hepatotoxicity
Phenytoin; progressive gingival hyperplasia
Ethosuximide; recurrent abdominal discomfort
Carbamazepine; severe marrow agranulocytosis
Lamotrigine; toxic epidermal necrolysis rash

explanation: Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis (ANC 200/µL presenting with fever and pharyngitis) and aplastic anemia are classic hematologic toxicities of carbamazepine, a first-line Na⁺-channel blocker for focal-onset seizures.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has 2 months of headache, social withdrawal, and low mood, and she has now developed urinary incontinence. An antidepressant gave no benefit. MRI shows an enhancing extra-axial right frontal mass with a dural tail. Which pairing of cell of origin and histology is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Astrocytes; pseudopalisading necrosis
Oligodendrocytes; fried-egg cells
Schwann cells; Antoni A and B areas
Ependymal cells; perivascular pseudorosettes
Arachnoid cap cells; whorls and psammoma bodies

explanation: An extra-axial dural-based mass with a dural tail is meningioma, arising from arachnoid cap cells with whorled spindle cells and psammoma bodies. It is more common in women and grows slowly, which explains the late onset of frontal behavioral and urinary symptoms.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has 3 days of blurred vision in the right eye with pain on eye movement. Two years ago she had transient numbness of the left leg that resolved without treatment. On the swinging-flashlight test, both pupils dilate when the light moves from the left eye to the right eye. MRI shows ovoid T2-hyperintense lesions perpendicular to the lateral ventricles. Which CSF finding is most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Albuminocytologic CSF dissociation
CSF oligoclonal IgG antibody bands
CSF xanthochromia from breakdown
Neutrophilic CSF with low glucose
Elevated CSF 14-3-3 brain protein

explanation: Step 1: pain on eye movement, an afferent pupillary defect on the right, a prior episode separated in time and space, and ovoid periventricular lesions indicate relapsing-remitting MS. Step 2: CSF in MS shows oligoclonal IgG bands (with a raised IgG index and myelin basic protein). Albuminocytologic dissociation is GBS, xanthochromia is SAH, neutrophils with low glucose is bacterial meningitis, and 14-3-3 is CJD.

stem: A 28-year-old woman taking phenytoin for focal seizures asks about pregnancy. Which fetal syndrome is most characteristic of this drug?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Lumbosacral neural tube defects alone
Ebstein tricuspid valve malformation
Cleft palate and hypoplastic fetal nails
Limb reduction phocomelia deformity
Isolated scalp aplasia cutis congenita

explanation: Phenytoin exposure in pregnancy causes fetal hydantoin syndrome, characterized by craniofacial abnormalities, cleft lip/palate, microcephaly, cardiac defects, developmental delay, and hypoplastic distal phalanges and nails.

stem: A 59-year-old man has a sudden severe headache followed by confusion and disorientation, with no focal deficits. Non-contrast CT shows blood throughout the subarachnoid space, and angiography shows a saccular aneurysm at an anterior cerebral artery branch point. Which complication should be monitored in the ICU over the next 2 weeks, and which drug lessens its consequences?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Epidural hematoma expansion; mannitol
Communicating hydrocephalus; nimodipine
Delayed cerebral vasospasm; nimodipine
Delayed cerebral vasospasm; IV alteplase
Aneurysmal rebleeding; antiplatelet aspirin

explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured anterior cerebral/anterior communicating saccular aneurysm places the patient at high risk for delayed cerebral vasospasm (peaking days 4–14 post-bleed). Prophylactic oral nimodipine (a dihydropyridine Ca²⁺ channel blocker) improves outcomes by preventing ischemic deficits from vasospasm.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 35-year-old man with epilepsy treated for 6 years has gingival overgrowth, coarse facial features, and increased facial and body hair. Which drug is most likely responsible?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Carbamazepine
Phenytoin
Valproic acid
Ethosuximide
Lamotrigine

explanation: Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, and coarsening of facial features (along with peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar ataxia in toxicity, osteomalacia, and folate-deficiency megaloblastic anemia) are classic chronic adverse effects of phenytoin.

stem: A 41-year-old woman has expressive aphasia with preserved comprehension, right-sided weakness with hyperreflexia and increased tone, a throbbing headache for 2 weeks, transient painless left monocular vision loss, and left ptosis with a smaller left pupil. Two weeks earlier she had a cosmetic neck procedure. MRI shows reduced flow in the left carotid artery. Which diagnosis and explanation of the left eye findings are correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Left vertebral dissection; lateral brainstem ischemia
Left MCA cardioembolism; central retinal artery infarct
Right ICA dissection; contralateral sympathetic injury
Left ICA dissection; ophthalmic ischemia and Horner syndrome
Left ACA thrombosis; ipsilateral frontal eye field lesion

explanation: Following neck trauma/manipulation, ipsilateral headache, transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax from ophthalmic artery ischemia), ipsilateral Horner syndrome (injury to oculosympathetic fibers ascending along the carotid sheath), and contralateral MCA hemispheric deficits (expressive aphasia, right hemiparesis) indicate left internal carotid artery (ICA) dissection.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 62-year-old woman has brief electric-shock facial pains in the V2 distribution, triggered by chewing and by light touch of the cheek. The first-line drug for this condition is also first-line for focal seizures. Which mechanism describes this drug?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Selective thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channel blockade
Use-dependent voltage-gated Na⁺ channel blockade
Direct irreversible GABA transaminase inhibition
Combined Na⁺/T-Ca²⁺ block and GABA elevation
Binding presynaptic vesicle glycoprotein SV2A

explanation: Carbamazepine is first-line therapy for trigeminal neuralgia as well as focal-onset seizures. It acts via use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, stabilizing the inactivated channel conformation.

stem: A 22-year-old man has progressive bilateral hearing loss. MRI shows bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses and a parasagittal meningioma. His father had similar tumors. Which gene, chromosome, and protein function are involved?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: NF1; chromosome 17; neurofibromin protein
NF2; chromosome 22; merlin cytoskeletal regulator
TSC1; chromosome 9; hamartin complex protein
TSC2; chromosome 16; tuberin complex protein
VHL; chromosome 3p; hypoxia factor regulator

explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas plus meningioma indicate NF2 (autosomal dominant), with the gene on chromosome 22 encoding merlin, which mediates contact inhibition of Schwann cell growth. NF1 is on chromosome 17 (neurofibromin), TSC1 on 9, TSC2 on 16, and VHL on 3p.

stem: A 66-year-old hypertensive man has sudden numbness of the entire left face, arm, and leg involving light touch, pain, and temperature. There is no weakness, cranial nerve palsy, ataxia, or crossed findings. Which structure and vessels are most likely involved?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Left posterior internal capsule; lenticulostriates
Right thalamic VPL/VPM nuclei; penetrating PCA branches
Right lateral medulla tegmentum; PICA trunk
Right pontine medial lemniscus; basilar branches
Left parietal sensory cortex; lateral MCA division

explanation: A pure sensory stroke affecting light touch, pain, and temperature across the entire contralateral (left) face, arm, and leg without motor weakness, ataxia, or cranial nerve palsies localizes to a lacunar infarct of the right thalamus (ventral posterolateral VPL and ventral posteromedial VPM nuclei) supplied by long penetrating branches (thalamogeniculate/thalamoperforator branches) of the PCA.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 10-year-old boy has both absence seizures and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Which pair of antiseizure drugs both act, at least in part, by blocking T-type calcium channels?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Carbamazepine and phenytoin
Ethosuximide and valproic acid
Phenytoin and lamotrigine
Carbamazepine and ethosuximide
Lamotrigine and carbamazepine

explanation: When absence seizures coexist with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, ethosuximide (selective thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channel blocker) and valproic acid (broad-spectrum: blocks Na⁺ channels, inhibits T-type Ca²⁺ channels, and raises GABA levels) both share T-type Ca²⁺ channel blockade; valproic acid covers both seizure types.

stem: A 70-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has stepwise cognitive decline after several small strokes, with prominent executive dysfunction and relatively late memory impairment. MRI shows multiple lacunes and confluent white matter hyperintensities. Which is the best management approach?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Ventriculoperitoneal CSF shunt surgery
VMAT2 inhibition with tetrabenazine
Empiric intravenous acyclovir therapy
High-dose systemic corticosteroid pulse
Aggressive vascular risk factor control

explanation: Stepwise cognitive deterioration, early prominent executive dysfunction, vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes), and multiple lacunes with confluent white matter hyperintensities characterize vascular dementia. The cornerstone of management is aggressive secondary prevention targeting modifiable vascular risk factors.

stem: A 64-year-old man has sudden difficulty chewing and unsteadiness. His jaw deviates to the left on opening. He has loss of light touch on the left face, loss of pain and temperature on the right body, left ptosis with a small left pupil, and left limb ataxia. Strength and eye movements are normal. Which cranial nerve marks the level, and which artery is occluded?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: CN V nerve; basilar circumferential branches
CN III nerve; posterior cerebral branches
CN VII nerve; anterior inferior cerebellar artery
CN XII nerve; anterior spinal artery branches
CN IX and X; posterior inferior cerebellar artery

explanation: Ipsilateral jaw deviation (LMN CN V motor), ipsilateral facial anesthesia (CN V sensory), ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral limb ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle), and contralateral body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic tract) localize to the lateral mid-pons supplied by circumferential branches of the basilar artery; CN V localizes the lesion specifically to the mid-pontine level.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 28-year-old man has headache and gait ataxia. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule, and fundoscopy reveals a retinal capillary hemangioma. His hemoglobin is 18.5 g/dL, and his father had renal cancer and a pheochromocytoma. Which chromosome and associated extra-CNS tumors are expected?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Chromosome 17; optic glioma and Lisch nodules
Chromosome 22; bilateral vestibular schwannomas
Chromosome 9; renal angiomyolipoma and cardiac rhabdomyoma
Chromosome 3p; clear cell renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
Chromosome 16; facial angiofibromas and shagreen patches

explanation: Cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas with renal cancer and pheochromocytoma in the family indicate von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL on chromosome 3p). Associated tumors are clear cell renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma, and hemangioblastoma erythropoietin production explains the high hemoglobin.

stem: A 20-year-old woman has 2 weeks of bilateral flank pain and episodic vomiting. She has facial angiofibromas, a leathery orange-peel patch on her lower back, and periungual fibromas, and she has had epilepsy since early childhood. CT shows both kidneys replaced by large lobulated masses with fat density. Which pairing correctly gives the genes and expected intracranial findings?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: NF1 on chromosome 17; optic gliomas and dermal fibromas
VHL on chromosome 3p; cerebellar hemangioblastoma lesions
GNAQ mosaic variant; ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma
NF2 on chromosome 22; bilateral vestibular schwannomas
TSC1 or TSC2; cortical tubers and subependymal nodules

explanation: Facial angiofibromas, a shagreen patch, periungual fibromas, epilepsy, and renal angiomyolipomas indicate tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 hamartin on chromosome 9, TSC2 tuberin on chromosome 16). Expect cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and possible subependymal giant cell astrocytoma.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with myoclonic and tonic-clonic seizures has been taking a drug that blocks Na⁺ and T-type Ca²⁺ channels and raises GABA levels. She now has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and an elevated serum lipase. Which pairing of adverse effect and drug is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Stevens-Johnson rash; lamotrigine
Gingival overgrowth; oral phenytoin
Hyponatremic SIADH; carbamazepine
Acute pancreatitis; valproic acid
Distal sensory loss; oral phenytoin

explanation: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated serum lipase in a patient taking valproic acid (blocks Na⁺/T-Ca²⁺ channels and elevates GABA) indicates drug-induced acute pancreatitis, a classic life-threatening adverse effect of valproic acid.

stem: A 19-year-old man with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy has been taking valproic acid for years. Lamotrigine is added and rapidly titrated. Ten days later he has fever, painful skin, mucosal erosions, and a diffuse blistering rash with epidermal detachment. Which drug and risk factor are most likely responsible?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Valproic acid monotherapy; slow upward titration
Ethosuximide; hepatic CYP450 enzyme induction
Carbamazepine; hepatic CYP450 autoinduction
Lamotrigine; rapid titration with valproate
Phenytoin; saturable zero-order elimination

explanation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (fever, painful skin, mucosal erosions, blistering, and epidermal detachment) shortly after adding lamotrigine—especially when titrated rapidly in a patient concurrently taking valproic acid—occurs because valproic acid inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and doubles its half-life.

stem: A 10-year-old girl has a year of burning leg pain and frequent tripping. Her mother has high arches. Exam shows pes cavus, hammer toes, atrophy of the distal leg muscles, 4/5 ankle dorsiflexion, reduced vibration sense below the ankles, and a steppage gait. Peroneal motor nerve conduction velocity is markedly slowed. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene
CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene
Tandem duplication of the PMP22 gene
Loss-of-function variant in the NF2 gene
Exon deletion in the dystrophin gene

explanation: Pes cavus, hammer toes, distal atrophy, steppage gait, and slowed conduction velocity indicate Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy). CMT1A is most often caused by a PMP22 duplication (autosomal dominant). GAA expansion in FXN is Friedreich ataxia, and CAG expansion in huntingtin is Huntington disease.

stem: A 75-year-old man with 25 years of poorly controlled hypertension has right face, arm, and leg weakness. He has no sensory loss, aphasia, or visual field defect. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows a small infarct in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule. Which vessel and pathology are most likely responsible?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Proximal left MCA trunk; cardiac embolus
Internal carotid artery; artery-to-artery embolus
Lenticulostriate vessels; chronic lipohyalinosis
Mid-basilar artery; local plaque thrombosis
Cortical bridging veins; shear acceleration tear

explanation: A pure motor hemiparesis affecting face, arm, and leg equally without cortical signs (no aphasia, neglect, or visual field defect) caused by a small infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule is a classic lacunar stroke. It results from lipohyalinosis (and microatheroma) of the deep penetrating lenticulostriate arteries due to chronic hypertension.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 58-year-old man has 8 months of disinhibition, inappropriate jokes, binge eating of sweets, and apathy. Memory is relatively preserved. MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Which pairing of pathologic protein and symptomatic treatment is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: α-Synuclein; cholinesterase inhibitors
β-Amyloid; anti-amyloid antibody
Prion protein; no effective treatment
Tau; SSRIs for behavioral symptoms
Huntingtin; tetrabenazine

explanation: Early personality change, behavioral disinhibition, apathy, hyperorality/binge eating of sweets, relative sparing of episodic memory early on, and frontal/anterior temporal atrophy define frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease). Histology commonly shows hyperphosphorylated tau inclusions (Pick bodies), and SSRIs help manage behavioral symptoms (cholinesterase inhibitors are typically ineffective and may worsen agitation).

stem: A 55-year-old man from Eastern Europe has 6 months of unsteady gait, bladder problems, and sharp, burning, paroxysmal leg pain. He has impaired vibration sense in the feet, a positive Romberg sign, absent leg reflexes, and a wide-based gait, but normal heel-to-shin testing and rapid alternating movements. FTA-ABS and CSF-VDRL are positive. Which structures are primarily damaged, and what is the treatment?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Cerebellar vermis neurons; IV penicillin G
Spinal anterior horn cells; supportive care
Dorsal roots and columns; vitamin B12
Dorsal roots and columns; IV penicillin G
Ventral motor nerve roots; IV immune globulin

explanation: A wide-based gait with a positive Romberg sign, absent reflexes, impaired vibration, and normal limb coordination is sensory ataxia. Positive FTA-ABS and CSF-VDRL establish tabes dorsalis, with demyelination of large-diameter fibers in the dorsal roots and dorsal columns. Treat with penicillin.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation collapses. Over the next hours he is awake and alert and follows commands with his eyes. He has no limb movement and cannot speak, swallow, or move his face or jaw. He can blink and move his eyes up and down. Which lesion and which preserved structures explain this presentation?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Bilateral lateral medulla; vestibular nuclear complex
Bilateral thalami; ascending somatosensory relay
Bilateral ventral pons; spared tegmentum and midbrain gaze
Bilateral midbrain tegmentum; paired red nuclei
Bilateral calcarine cortex; primary visual areas

explanation: Preserved consciousness, intact blinking, and preserved vertical eye movements with complete quadriplegia, anarthria, and loss of horizontal gaze define locked-in syndrome. Occlusion of the basilar trunk infarcts the bilateral ventral pons (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts plus horizontal gaze pathways) while sparing the pontine tegmental reticular activating system and midbrain vertical gaze centers.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: A 24-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is well controlled on valproic acid and plans to become pregnant. Which fetal risk is most characteristic of this drug, and which supplement is recommended?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Fetal hydantoin syndrome; vitamin K
Fetal hyponatremia; sodium supplementation
Neural tube defects; high-dose folate
Aplastic anemia in the infant; iron
Isolated cleft palate; vitamin D

explanation: Valproic acid carries the highest teratogenic risk of neural tube defects (spina bifida) among common antiseizure drugs; high-dose folic acid supplementation (4 mg/day) is recommended before conception and during early pregnancy if valproate cannot be avoided.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has trouble controlling her left arm. Her hand shakes as it approaches her fork, she misses her mouth, and she cannot rapidly flip her left hand over and back. Left finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin are inaccurate, and her speech is slurred, but strength and comprehension are normal. Which lesion location and output pathway best explain her findings?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Left cerebellar hemisphere; dentate nucleus via superior peduncle
Right cerebellar hemisphere; dentate nucleus via superior peduncle
Left cerebellar vermis; fastigial nucleus via inferior peduncle
Left flocculonodular lobe; fastigial nucleus via inferior peduncle
Right primary motor cortex; descending lateral corticospinal tract

explanation: Ipsilateral limb ataxia, kinetic tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and dysarthria localize to the left cerebellar hemisphere (cerebrocerebellum). Its output leaves through the dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle. The cerebrocerebellar circuit crosses twice, so signs are ipsilateral to the lesion.

stem: At autopsy, a 65-year-old man with 20 years of heavy alcohol use and a wide-based gait has atrophy of the cerebellar vermis. Microscopy shows loss of the neurons that provide the sole output of the cerebellar cortex. Which pairing identifies these cells and the neurotransmitter they use on the deep cerebellar nuclei?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Granule cell interneurons; glutamate
Cerebellar Purkinje cells; glutamate
Golgi inhibitory interneurons; glycine
Cerebellar Purkinje neurons; GABA
Inferior olivary climbing fibers; GABA

explanation: Purkinje cells are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex and use GABA to inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei. Alcohol-related cerebellar atrophy causes Purkinje cell loss.

stem: A 3-month-old infant has a port-wine stain over the right forehead and upper eyelid and begins having focal seizures. Ophthalmology finds elevated intraocular pressure on the right. Head CT shows gyral “tram-track” calcifications. Which pairing of genetic mechanism and pathology is correct?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Germline TSC2 variant; subependymal cortical tubers
Mosaic GNAQ variant; cortical leptomeningeal angioma
NF2 loss on chromosome 22; convexities meningioma
VHL deletion on 3p; cerebellar hemangioblastoma
Germline NF1 variant; cutaneous plexiform neurofibroma

explanation: A facial port-wine stain, seizures, glaucoma, and tram-track gyral calcifications indicate Sturge-Weber syndrome, caused by a mosaic GNAQ mutation, with leptomeningeal (arachnoid-pia) angiomas.

stem: A 36-year-old man has new-onset seizures. MRI shows a nonenhancing infiltrative mass in the left frontal lobe. Biopsy shows a hypercellular, GFAP-positive tumor with nuclear atypia but no mitotic activity, necrosis, or microvascular proliferation. Which WHO grade and biologic behavior are expected?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Grade I; circumscribed lesion often cured by resection
Grade II; infiltrative growth risking higher progression
Grade III; anaplastic neoplasm with frequent mitoses
Grade IV; high-grade lesion with central necrosis
Grade I; cystic cerebellar mass seen in childhood

explanation: A hypercellular GFAP-positive tumor with nuclear atypia but no mitoses, necrosis, or microvascular proliferation is a diffuse (infiltrating) astrocytoma, WHO grade II. It typically presents with seizures at age 30–40, infiltrates diffusely, and can progress to anaplastic astrocytoma or glioblastoma.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with aggressive MS has been on immunosuppressive therapy for 2 years. She develops progressive visual loss, cognitive decline, behavioral change, and unsteadiness. MRI shows nonenhancing white matter lesions in both parieto-occipital regions without mass effect, and CSF is positive for JC virus DNA. Which cell type is directly infected, and which pathology results?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Astrocytes; diffuse neuronal phagocytosis
Cortical neurons; diffuse spongiform change
Schwann cells; peripheral nerve demyelination
CNS microglia; perivascular microglial nodules
Oligodendrocytes; focal CNS white demyelination

explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is caused by reactivation of JC virus in immunocompromised patients (e.g., natalizumab-treated MS or AIDS). JC virus selectively infects oligodendrocytes, causing patchy, nonenhancing parieto-occipital white matter demyelination without mass effect and lipid-laden macrophages along with enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei containing viral inclusions.

stem: A 52-year-old man has taken phenytoin for 10 years. He has fatigue, macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, low serum folate, and numbness in a stocking distribution. Which adverse-effect pair of phenytoin best explains these findings?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Aplastic anemia and drug-induced SIADH
Microangiopathic hemolysis and liver failure
Marrow agranulocytosis and pancreatitis
Pure red cell aplasia and hepatic steatosis
Folate-deficiency anemia and neuropathy

explanation: Long-term phenytoin impairs intestinal folate absorption and accelerates hepatic metabolism, causing folate-deficiency megaloblastic anemia; chronic therapy also frequently causes a symmetric stocking-glove peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 33-year-old man presented with 4 days of progressive symmetric leg weakness, tingling, absent patellar and ankle reflexes, and a history of diarrhea 4 weeks earlier after eating undercooked chicken. Two days after admission he develops shortness of breath, and his forced vital capacity is falling. Which is the most appropriate management, and what best explains why recovery is generally favorable in this disorder?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: IV methylprednisolone; oligodendrocytes remyelinate rapidly
Plasma exchange or IVIG; Schwann cells proliferate reliably
Plasma exchange or IVIG; oligodendrocytes remyelinate rapidly
IV methylprednisolone; Schwann cells proliferate reliably
Interferon-β therapy; central CNS neurons regenerate rapidly

explanation: Treatment is plasma exchange or IVIG, and steroids are not indicated. Monitor FVC for respiratory failure. Prognosis is generally good because Schwann cells can proliferate and remyelinate, unlike oligodendrocytes in central demyelinating disease.

stem: An 18-year-old man has progressive gait ataxia, scoliosis, pes cavus, absent ankle reflexes, loss of vibration sense, and a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on echocardiogram. Which pairing identifies the molecular defect and its cellular consequence?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: CAG repeat in HTT; striatal huntingtin aggregation
GAA repeat in FXN; frataxin loss and iron overload
PMP22 duplication; defective peripheral compact myelin
GAA repeat in FXN; lysosomal ganglioside storage
Variant in SOD1; motor neuron excitotoxic injury

explanation: Ataxia, scoliosis, pes cavus, absent reflexes, vibration loss, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy indicate Friedreich ataxia. A GAA repeat expansion in FXN reduces frataxin, causing mitochondrial iron accumulation and degeneration of the dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts.

stem: A 79-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease becomes acutely confused over 2 days after developing pneumonia. He is inattentive, drowsy by day, agitated at night, and has disorganized speech. Which feature best indicates delirium rather than dementia progression, and what is the next step?
source: Neuro Exam 3 In House c (100 Qs)

options.text: Gradual decline over months; add memantine
Normal attention span; increase donepezil dose
Stepwise worsening course; aspirin and statin
Abrupt fluctuating attention; treat precipitant
Rapid course with myoclonus; check 14-3-3 protein

explanation: Abrupt onset over hours to days, impaired attention, and a fluctuating level of consciousness/sleep-wake reversal in the setting of acute infection (pneumonia) distinguish delirium from progression of underlying dementia. Primary management is identifying and treating the underlying medical precipitant.
